title: How Sarcasm Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore sarcasm: how it differs from verbal irony, its ancient Greek roots and Socratic irony, how people detect it (tone, nasal delivery, eye rolls, elongation, context), children's and neurodivergent understanding of sarcasm (including autism and dementia), theories for why people use it (Tinge theory, politeness theory, the biting-criticism theory, humor), its role in literature, its risks in marriage and written communication (John Gottman's four horsemen), and claimed creativity and social benefits. The episode ends with a listener email about Elton John's song "Ticking."

segments.title: Opening banter and sarcasm vs. verbal irony
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter, then discuss how hard sarcasm is to produce on purpose and how it can hide emotions or conflict. They distinguish sarcasm, which is insulting or mocking, from verbal irony, using a meteorologist example.

segments.title: Definition and Socratic irony
segments.summary: The Oxford English Dictionary definition of sarcasm is discussed, including its Greek root meaning to tear flesh. The hosts describe Socratic irony and its namesake, Socrates.

segments.title: Clues for detecting sarcasm
segments.summary: Listeners pick up sarcasm from tone of voice, nasal delivery, eye rolls, intonation (inverse pitch obtrusion), elongating or deflating words, and cultural differences such as sarcasm in Japan. Learning English with sitcoms is mentioned.

segments.title: Children, neurodiversity, and dementia
segments.summary: Research suggests children start recognizing sarcasm around age six and understand it as humor around age ten. A 2005 French study is mentioned. People with dementia, brain lesions, and autism may have difficulty with sarcasm, linked to literal thinking and theory of mind.

segments.title: Brain processing of sarcasm
segments.summary: A 2005 study is described that identifies three brain regions involved in processing sarcasm: the language cortex, the frontal lobes and right hemisphere, and the right ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Sarcasm is framed as unplain speaking.

segments.title: Why people use sarcasm: Tinge and politeness theories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why sarcasm is used when a direct message would work. The Tinge theory and politeness theory say it softens criticism or praise. The opposing view holds that sarcasm makes criticism more biting. Sarcasm as a social lubricant is discussed, along with the idea that it is simply humor and Oscar Wilde's quote on wit.

segments.title: Sarcasm in literature and the Bible
segments.summary: Sarcasm in Mark Twain, Shakespeare, and Chaucer is mentioned. The hosts read Ecclesiastes 11:9 and debate whether it is sarcasm. Written text makes sarcasm harder to read.

segments.title: Sarcasm in texts, emails, and relationships
segments.summary: Studies find people overestimate how clearly their sarcasm comes through in texts and emails. Emoji and tags are suggested. Therapists regard sarcasm as veiled hostility, and John Gottman lists it as a sign of contempt and a predictor of divorce. The hosts describe a stepfather who is excessively sarcastic.

segments.title: Benefits of sarcasm and the Michael Richards apology
segments.summary: A study linking sarcasm to higher creativity scores is discussed with skepticism. Other claimed benefits include social bonding, egalitarianism, and perceived competence at work, per Harvard Business Review. The hosts recall Michael Richards' apology on Letterman, which some audience members took as sarcasm.

segments.title: Listener mail: Elton John's Ticking
segments.summary: A listener from Fort Worth, Texas, writes that Elton John's song Ticking, from the Caribou album, predicted future shooting events. The hosts discuss it, along with Stephen King's short story and the film Falling Down.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and give the email address for contacting the show.
